objectives.text: The learner can trace binary search by hand on a small sorted array
The learner can explain why it needs a sorted input
The learner can say why it is log n rather than n

say: You already know this algorithm. It is how you look up a word in a paper dictionary: open in the middle, decide which half it is in, throw the other half away, repeat. The only trick is being precise about the bookkeeping.

board.text: Looking for 23. Low is 0, high is 6.

say: Middle of nought to six is three, which holds twelve. Twenty three is bigger, so everything at or below index three is gone. Low becomes four. Middle is now five, which holds twenty three. Found, in two comparisons.

board.text: Seven elements, two comparisons. A scan from the left would have taken six.

say: Here is the same thing in code. The line worth staring at is the one computing the middle, and notice that low and high move past each other, which is what ends the loop when the value is simply not there.

board.text: In a language with fixed-width integers, lo + hi can overflow. lo + (hi - lo) // 2 cannot.

questions.q: Why must the array be sorted?
options: Otherwise the middle element is undefined
Otherwise comparing to the middle tells you nothing about which half to keep
It does not have to be sorted
questions.why: The whole algorithm rests on one comparison ruling out half the array. Unsorted, that comparison rules out nothing.

questions.q: How many comparisons does binary search need on a million sorted items, worst case?
questions.why: Each comparison halves the range, and 2 to the 20 is about a million.

say: That second answer is the whole point. Each comparison halves what is left. So the question becomes how many times you can halve a million before you reach one, and that is exactly what a logarithm counts.

lines.note: k is the number of comparisons

board.text: Going from a thousand items to a billion costs ten more comparisons. That is what logarithmic means.

summary: We traced binary search by hand, read the implementation, saw why sorting is a precondition rather than a convenience, and derived the log n comparison count.
